title: CSC3710 2026-09-08: Set concatenation, powers, Kleene star, languages, regular sets

questions.q: Let X = {a, ab, λ} and Y = {λ, b, a}. How many distinct strings are in the concatenation XY?
questions.explain: XY = {λ, a, b, aa, ab, aba, abb}. The string a comes from both a·λ and λ·a, and ab comes from both a·b and ab·λ, so the 9 pairs produce only 7 distinct strings.

questions.q: Let X = {a, ab, λ} and Y = {λ, b, a}. How many elements are in the Cartesian product X × Y?
questions.explain: X × Y is a set of ordered pairs, and distinct pairs never collide, so |X × Y| = |X| · |Y| = 3 · 3 = 9.

questions.q: Let X = {a, ab} and Y = {λ, b}. What is XY?
questions.explain: a·λ = a, a·b = ab, ab·λ = ab, ab·b = abb. Drop λ and the repeated ab to get {a, ab, abb}. {a, ab, ba, bab} is YX, and the set of pairs is X × Y.

questions.q: For all finite sets of strings X and Y, |XY| ≤ |X| · |Y|.
questions.explain: Each pair (x, y) gives exactly one string xy, but different pairs can give the same string, so XY can have fewer elements than X × Y, never more. Equality is possible, e.g. X = {a}, Y = {b}.

questions.q: Why can XY have fewer elements than X × Y?
choices: Different pairs (x, y) can produce the same string xy
Concatenation removes every string that contains λ
XY only includes strings where x ≠ y
The Cartesian product counts each pair twice
questions.explain: Pairs such as (a, λ) and (λ, a) are different elements of X × Y, but both produce the single string a in XY.

questions.q: Which pair of strings are equal?
questions.explain: λ is the empty string, so concatenating it changes nothing: aλb = ab. Strings are ordered sequences, so aa ≠ a and ab ≠ ba.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes XY from X × Y?
choices: They are the same set written two different ways
XY is a set of strings; X × Y is a set of ordered pairs
XY is a set of ordered pairs; X × Y is a set of strings
XY is defined only for alphabets; X × Y is defined for any sets
questions.explain: XY = {xy | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y} contains strings. X × Y = {(x, y) | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y} contains ordered pairs.

questions.q: Set concatenation is commutative: XY = YX for all sets of strings X and Y.
questions.explain: Counterexample: {a}{b} = {ab} but {b}{a} = {ba}. The order of the parts matters.

questions.q: For any set of strings X, what is X∅?
questions.explain: Every string in X∅ needs a second part taken from ∅, and ∅ has nothing in it, so no strings can be formed. X∅ = ∅X = ∅.

questions.q: Which set E is the identity for set concatenation, meaning XE = EX = X for every X?
questions.explain: Concatenating with {λ} attaches the empty string, so each x stays x. ∅ behaves like 0 (it annihilates), {λ} behaves like 1.

questions.q: Which statements hold for all sets of strings X, Y, Z?
questions.explain: Concatenation is associative, {λ} is the identity, and ∅ annihilates. It is not commutative in general, and X∅ is ∅, not X.

questions.q: Which pair of sets is a counterexample showing that concatenation is not commutative?
questions.explain: XY = {ab} but YX = {ba}. In the other choices XY = YX (Y = {λ} or ∅ are special cases, and X = Y trivially commutes).

questions.q: Since X∅ = ∅X and X{λ} = {λ}X for every X, the general statement 'set concatenation is commutative' is true.
questions.explain: Those are special cases. A general claim must hold for all X and Y, and it fails for X = {a}, Y = {b}.

questions.q: Why is X∅ = ∅ for every set of strings X?
choices: λ is removed from every string during concatenation
Every string in X∅ needs a second part taken from ∅, and ∅ has no elements
∅ is the identity element for concatenation
X∅ is defined to be ∅ only when X is infinite
questions.explain: Just as X × ∅ = ∅ because no pairs can be formed, no strings xy can be formed when there is no y to choose.

questions.q: By the basis of the recursive definition of powers of a set, X⁰ equals:
questions.explain: X⁰ = {λ} for every set X, including X = ∅. Note that λ by itself is a string, not a set.

questions.q: Which is the recursive step in the definition of Xⁿ?
questions.explain: Each power is the previous power concatenated with X. Union would not lengthen strings, and × would produce pairs, not strings.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. What is Σ²?
choices: {λ, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb}
questions.explain: Σ² = Σ¹Σ = {a, b}{a, b} = {aa, ab, ba, bb}, all strings of length exactly 2. ab and ba are different strings.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. How many strings are in Σ³?
questions.explain: Σ³ = Σ²Σ = {aaa, aab, aba, abb, baa, bab, bba, bbb}. In general {a, b}ⁿ has 2ⁿ strings.

questions.q: What is {ab, b}²?
questions.explain: {ab, b}² = {ab, b}{ab, b}: ab·ab = abab, ab·b = abb, b·ab = bab, b·b = bb. All four are distinct.

questions.q: What is ∅⁰?
questions.explain: The basis X⁰ = {λ} applies to every set, including the empty set.

questions.q: What is ∅¹?
questions.explain: ∅¹ = ∅⁰∅ = {λ}∅ = ∅, because concatenating with ∅ always gives ∅.

questions.q: In words, {a, b}ⁿ is:
choices: all strings over {a, b} of length exactly n
all strings over {a, b} of length at most n
all strings over {a, b} with exactly n a's
the n-th string of Σ* listed in order of length
questions.explain: Each application of the recursive step appends one symbol, so {a, b}ⁿ is exactly the strings of length n.

questions.q: Which is the definition of X* (Kleene star)?
questions.explain: X* is the union of all powers Xⁱ for i ≥ 0. Starting at X¹ instead gives X⁺.

questions.q: What is ∅*?
questions.explain: ∅⁰ = {λ} and every higher power is ∅, so ∅* = {λ} ∪ ∅ ∪ ∅ ∪ … = {λ}.

questions.q: What is {λ}*?
questions.explain: {λ}⁰ = {λ}, and {λ}ᵏ = {λ}{λ} = {λ} for every k, so the union is just {λ}.

questions.q: λ ∈ X* for every set X, including X = ∅.
questions.explain: X* includes X⁰ = {λ}, and that holds for every set.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Then λ ∈ Σ⁺.
questions.explain: Σ⁺ = Σ*Σ consists of one or more symbols, so every string has length at least 1. Σ⁺ = Σ* − {λ}.

questions.q: Which of the following equal X⁺ for every set X?
questions.explain: X⁺ = XX* = X*X. X⁺ equals X* only when λ ∈ X, and equals X* − {λ} only when λ ∉ X.
λ ∈ {λ, a} = X¹ ⊆ X⁺. 'X⁺ has no λ' holds only when λ ∉ X.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Listed in order of length, what are the shortest elements of Σ*Σ?
choices: a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, …
questions.explain: Σ*Σ = Σ⁺: every string over {a, b} except λ. The shortest are λa = a and λb = b.

questions.q: For which sets X is X* a finite set?
questions.explain: ∅* = {λ}* = {λ}. Any other X contains a nonempty string w, so w, ww, www, … are all in X*.

questions.q: In the recursive definition of Σ*, what is the basis?
choices: a ∈ Σ* for some a ∈ Σ
questions.explain: The basis puts the empty string in Σ*. Everything else is built from λ by the recursive step.

questions.q: Which is the recursive step in the definition of Σ*?
choices: If w ∈ Σ and a ∈ Σ*, then wa ∈ Σ
If w ∈ Σ* and a ∈ Σ, then wa ∈ Σ*
If w ∈ Σ*, then ww ∈ Σ*
If w ∈ Σ*, then w ∪ Σ ∈ Σ*
questions.explain: w is a string already in Σ*, a is a single symbol of the alphabet, and appending a to w gives a new string in Σ*.

questions.q: By the usual naming convention, which letters stand for strings rather than symbols?
choices: Letters from the start of the English alphabet (a, b, c, d)
Letters from the end of the English alphabet (u, v, w, x, y, z)
questions.explain: Lowercase letters from the start (a, b, c, d) denote symbols; lowercase letters from the end (u through z) denote strings. That is why the recursive step uses w for a string and a for a symbol.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which sequence of strings uses the recursive definition of Σ* correctly to show bba ∈ Σ*?
questions.explain: Start with λ (basis), then append one symbol at the right end each time: λb = b, b·b = bb, bb·a = bba. Going from a to ba or from ba to bba would require adding a symbol on the left, which the rule wa does not do.

questions.q: A language over an alphabet Σ is defined as:
choices: any nonempty set of strings over Σ
questions.explain: Any subset of Σ* is a language, including finite ones, ∅, {λ}, and Σ* itself.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which of these are languages over Σ?
questions.explain: Each is a subset of Σ*, except {c}: c ∉ Σ, so the string c is not in Σ*. Σ* is a subset of itself, and ∅ is a subset of every set.

questions.q: ∅ and {λ} are the same language.
questions.explain: ∅ contains no strings. {λ} contains exactly one string, the empty string of length 0.

questions.q: The empty set is not a language, because it contains no strings.
questions.explain: Go by the definition: ∅ ⊆ Σ*, so ∅ is a language. It is just not an interesting one.

questions.q: The set of all languages over Σ is:
questions.explain: Each language is a subset of Σ*, so the collection of all languages is the set of all subsets of Σ*, which is 𝒫(Σ*). Since Σ* is countably infinite, 𝒫(Σ*) is uncountable.

questions.q: When English is modeled as a formal language (with sentences as strings), what is the alphabet?
choices: The 26 letters of the English alphabet
The set of English words, each treated as an indivisible symbol
The set of grammatical English sentences
questions.explain: Each English word is one symbol. Words such as 'eat' and 'ate' are separate, unrelated symbols even though grammar connects them.

questions.q: For a programming language such as Java or Python, an alphabet containing the keywords and all possible identifiers is very large but finite.
questions.explain: Naming rules (for example, no '=' in a name) and a limit on identifier length keep the set of possible identifiers finite.

questions.q: A string over an alphabet Σ is:
choices: a finite sequence of symbols from Σ
an infinite sequence of symbols from Σ
an unordered collection of symbols from Σ
questions.explain: Strings are finite and ordered. For example, a digital photograph is stored as a finite bit string over {0, 1}.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which sets are in the basis of the recursive definition of regular sets over Σ?
questions.explain: The basis is ∅, {λ}, and {x} for each symbol x ∈ Σ. {a, b} and Σ* are regular, but they come from the recursive step ({a} ∪ {b}, then star).

questions.q: Which operations appear in the recursive step of the definition of regular sets?
questions.explain: If X and Y are regular, then X ∪ Y, XY, and X* are regular. These three operations are all the definition uses.

questions.q: Starting from the basis sets over Σ = {a, b}, which derivation correctly produces the regular set {ab, bb}?
choices: {a, b} is a basis set; concatenate {a, b}{b}
questions.explain: {a, b}{b} = {ab, bb}. {a, b} is not a basis set; it has to be built by union. {ab}* is a different set, and {b}{a} ∪ {b}{b} = {ba, bb}.

questions.q: Listed in order of length, what are the shortest elements of {ab, bb}*?
choices: λ, ab, bb, abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb, …
ab, bb, abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb, …
questions.explain: {ab, bb}⁰ = {λ}, {ab, bb}¹ = {ab, bb}, {ab, bb}² = {abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb}. These are strings built from ab and bb as blocks, including zero blocks.

questions.q: How many strings of length 4 are in {ab, bb}*?
questions.explain: Length-4 strings come from two blocks: {ab, bb}² = {abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb}.

questions.q: Which strings are in {ab, bb}*?
questions.explain: Every string must split into blocks ab and bb. ba and aabb cannot be split this way, and abb has odd length. λ uses zero blocks.

questions.q: Which derivation shows that {a, ba}* is a regular set?
choices: {a, ba} is a basis set; then take the star
questions.explain: Concatenate basis sets {b} and {a} to get {ba}, union with {a}, then apply star. {a}{b} is {ab}, not {ba}, and {a, b}* is a different set.

questions.q: Regex shortcuts such as a{10} (a repeated 10 times) let you describe sets that union, concatenation, and Kleene star cannot.
questions.explain: Such shortcuts are conveniences. a{10} is just a concatenated with itself 10 times. Union, concatenation, and star already capture every regular set.

questions.q: Each application of the recursive step in the definition of regular sets produces a set that has not been generated before.
questions.explain: The result is not necessarily new. For example, {a} ∪ {a} = {a}, and ∅* = {λ} is already a basis set.

questions.q: Every language over Σ = {a, b} is regular.
questions.explain: Each regular set has a finite derivation, so there are only countably many regular sets, but there are uncountably many languages (𝒫(Σ*) is uncountable).

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {a, b}*{a}?
choices: All strings that end with a
All strings that start with a
All strings with exactly one a
questions.explain: Any string (possibly λ) followed by a. Shortest elements: a, aa, ba, aaa, aba, baa, bba, …

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {aa, ab, ba, bb}*?
choices: All strings of even length except λ
All strings with an even number of a's
All strings of even length, including λ
questions.explain: The blocks are all four strings of length 2, so any even-length string can be built. λ has length 0, which is even, and is in the set from the star.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {b}{a, b}*?
choices: All strings that end with b
All strings that start with b
All strings containing exactly one b
questions.explain: A b comes first, followed by λ or any string of a's and b's: b, ba, bb, baa, bab, …

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {a, b}*{aa}{a, b}*?
choices: Strings that start with a or b, followed by aa, followed by a or b
All strings that contain aa as a substring
All strings that start and end with a
All strings with exactly two a's
questions.explain: Each side can be any string, including λ, so aa alone is in the set and the set is infinite. The first choice describes {a, b}{aa}{a, b}, the version without stars, which has only 4 strings.

questions.q: How many strings are in {a, b}{aa}{a, b}?
questions.explain: {a, b}{aa}{a, b} = {aaaa, aaab, baaa, baab}. Without stars, each side contributes exactly one symbol.

questions.q: Which strings belong to {a, b}*{aa}{a, b}*?
questions.explain: The set is all strings containing the substring aa. abab and aba have no two a's in a row, and λ has no aa.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in {a, b}*{a}?
questions.explain: Take λ from {a, b}* and concatenate with a: λa = a. λ itself is not in the set, because every string ends with a.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {a, b}{aa, ab, ba, bb}*?
choices: All strings of length at least 2
All strings that start with a
questions.explain: One symbol followed by an even-length string gives odd length: a, b, aaa, aab, aba, …

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which English description matches {a}{a, b}*{b}?
choices: All strings that start with a and end with b
All strings that start with b and end with a
questions.explain: An a, then any string (possibly λ), then a b: ab, aab, abb, aaab, aabb, … The string bab contains ab but does not start with a, so 'contains ab' is not precise.

questions.q: λ ∈ {aa, ab, ba, bb}*.
questions.explain: Every starred set contains λ, from X⁰ = {λ}.

questions.q: Regular expressions are best described as:
choices: programs that run on Turing machines
a more powerful kind of set than regular sets
complete lists of the strings in a language
questions.explain: A regular expression drops the braces, writes ∪ for union, places parts side by side for concatenation, and uses * for star. It is shorthand for a regular set.

questions.q: Which regular expression denotes all strings over {a, b} that contain aa as a substring?
questions.explain: This abbreviates {a, b}*{aa}{a, b}*. Without the stars you get only 4 strings of length 4; aa(a ∪ b)* only covers strings that start with aa.

questions.q: Which regular expression denotes all strings over {a, b} that start with b?
questions.explain: b(a ∪ b)* abbreviates {b}{a, b}*. (a ∪ b)* b gives strings ending with b.

questions.q: Which regular expression denotes all strings over {a, b} that end with a?
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)* a abbreviates {a, b}*{a}: any string followed by a.

questions.q: Which regular set does (ab ∪ bb)* denote?
questions.explain: ab ∪ bb is {ab, bb}, and the star applies to the whole union. {ab}*{bb}* is different: it does not contain bbab.

questions.q: Which regular expression denotes all strings of even length over {a, b}?
questions.explain: Any number of length-2 blocks gives every even length, including 0. (aa ∪ bb)* misses strings like ab, (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) only has length 2, and (a ∪ b)*(a ∪ b)* is all strings.

questions.q: Many regex tools write union with a vertical bar, because ∪ is hard to type. How is (a ∪ b)* aa (a ∪ b)* written in that notation?
questions.explain: | stands for ∪. Using + instead of * would require at least one symbol on each side, so aa itself would be excluded.
